We hypothesize that CDS1 inhibition leads to increased levels of the oncogenic protein C/EBPβ in hepatocytes, which in turn causes hepatocellular carcinoma. We hypothesize that PLCG1 deficiency leads to combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria through a mechanism involving the accumulation of methylmalonic acid. We hypothesize that CYP2A13 is a key enzyme in the metabolism of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (25OHD3) in humans. 25OHD3 is a prohormone that is hydroxylated by CYP2R1 in the liver to form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25OHD3), the active form of vitamin D3. 1,25OHD3 is known to be involved in bone growth and development. terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CERS1 deficiency leads to Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1. CERS1 is a ceramide synthase that catalyzes the synthesis of ceramide, a key component of sphingolipids. Sphingolipids are essential for mitochondrial function, and their dysregulation has been implicated in mitochondrial disease. We propose that CERS1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of toxic intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism, which in turn impair mitochondrial complex II function. This would result in a deficiency of complex II activity, which is characteristic of Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1.

We hypothesize that GADL1, a glutamate decarboxylase, is a causative gene for Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5. GADL1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of glutamate to γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the brain. We propose that a mutation in GADL1 disrupts the conversion of glutamate to GABA, leading to an accumulation of glutamate in the kidney. Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter that can cause vasoconstriction and hypertension when present in high concentrations. We predict that patients with mutations in GADL1 will have elevated levels of glutamate in the kidney, which can be measured by mass spectrometry. This would provide evidence that GADL1 is a causative gene for Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5.

We hypothesize that HMOX1 is a causative gene for pontocerebellar hypoplasia 12 (PCH12). The UPR is a cellular response to ER stress that aims to restore homeostasis by increasing the production of ER chaperones and decreasing the amount of protein being made. We predict that patients with Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency will have higher levels of ROS than controls. This can be tested by measuring the levels of ROS in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency and controls using flow cytometry.

We hypothesize that CYP11A1 is involved in the pathogenesis of Aminoacylase-1 deficiency. CYP11A1 is a cytochrome P450 enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, the precursor of all steroid hormones. Pregnenolone is a substrate for aminoacylase-1, which hydrolyzes it to pregnanolone. Pregnanolone is a neurosteroid that modulates the activity of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) A receptor. GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. Mutations in the aminoacylase-1 gene cause a deficiency of this enzyme, leading to an accumulation of pregnenolone and other neurosteroids. This accumulation may cause an imbalance in the GABAergic system, leading to epilepsy. CYP11A1 deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the absence of pregnenolone synthesis. It is caused by mutations in the CYP11A1 gene, which encodes the enzyme steroid 11-beta-hydroxylase. CYP11A1 deficiency is associated with a wide range of clinical manifestations, including adrenal insufficiency, hyperkalemia, hypertension, and hypogonadism. We predict that patients with CYP11A1 deficiency will have lower levels of aminoacylase-1 activity compared to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that mutations in the gene encoding COX10, a mitochondrial enzyme involved in heme biosynthesis, lead to Desbuquois dysplasia 1. COX10 catalyzes the conversion of 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) to coproporphyrinogen III, an essential step in heme biosynthesis. Mutations in the gene encoding COX10 have been associated with heme biosynthesis defects, including acute intermittent porphyria and porphyria cutanea tarda. Desbuquois dysplasia 1 is a rare genetic disorder characterized by skeletal dysplasia, intellectual disability, and facial dysmorphism. Recent studies have implicated heme biosynthesis defects in the pathogenesis of Desbuquois dysplasia 1. We predict that mutations in the gene encoding COX10 will be associated with Desbuquois dysplasia 1. This hypothesis can be tested by sequencing the gene encoding COX10 in patients with Desbuquois dysplasia 1.

We hypothesize that ABCC1, a multidrug resistance protein, is a causative factor in Methemoglobinemia CYB5R3-related. ABCC1 is a member of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter family, which is responsible for the efflux of various substrates, including toxins and drugs. We propose that ABCC1 is involved in the efflux of methemoglobin (MetHb), a toxic byproduct of hemoglobin oxidation. MetHb is formed when iron in the heme group of hemoglobin is oxidized from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the ferric (Fe3+) state. MetHb is unable to bind oxygen and can cause tissue hypoxia. We predict that in Methemoglobinemia CYB5R3-related, ABCC1 is overexpressed, leading to increased efflux of MetHb from the cell. This would result in lower levels of MetHb in the red blood cells, leading to decreased tissue hypoxia and improved symptoms of the disease. To test this hypothesis, we would measure the expression levels of ABCC1 in patients with Methemoglobinemia CYB5R3-related and healthy controls. We would also perform efflux assays using MetHb as a substrate to determine if ABCC1 is involved in the efflux of MetHb.

terminal_shown: Salt and pepper developmental regression syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that LCLAT1 is a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter dopamine. In the brain, dopamine is synthesized from tyrosine by the enzymes tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC). LCLAT1 is a cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of L-leucine to isoleucine. It is expressed in the brain, and its expression is increased in the presence of dopamine. We hypothesize that LCLAT1 is involved in the biosynthesis of dopamine by providing the precursor L-leucine. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that L-leucine is a precursor of dopamine, and that LCLAT1 is expressed in the brain. We predict that the expression of LCLAT1 is increased in the presence of dopamine, and that the expression of LCLAT1 is decreased in the presence of dopamine receptor antagonists. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that LCLAT1 is a cytosolic enzyme, and that dopamine receptors are located on the cell membrane.

We hypothesize that GAS6 is a key regulator of lipid metabolism in Schwann cells, and that its dysfunction in these cells contributes to the pathogenesis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2U. Schwann cells are myelin-forming cells that wrap around axons in the peripheral nervous system. In the absence of functional Schwann cells, axons are unable to properly myelinate, leading to a loss of signal conduction and ultimately to axonal degeneration.

We hypothesize that AGMAT deficiency leads to the accumulation of urocanic acid in the urine, which in turn leads to the formation of urocanate-derived AGEs. These AGEs can cross-link with proteins in the kidney, leading to kidney damage and kidney failure. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that AGMAT deficiency is associated with the accumulation of urocanic acid in the urine, and that AGEs are known to cause kidney damage.

We hypothesize that TPMT, an enzyme involved in thymine metabolism, is the source enzyme for Leber congenital amaurosis 14. TPMT catalyzes the conversion of thymine to thymine monophosphate, which is then converted to thymidine monophosphate. Thymidine monophosphate is a precursor for the synthesis of DNA. We propose that mutations in TPMT lead to decreased TPMT activity, resulting in decreased thymidine monophosphate levels. Decreased thymidine monophosphate levels can lead to decreased DNA synthesis, resulting in cell death. This would explain the retinal degeneration seen in Leber congenital amaurosis 14.

We hypothesize that the source enzyme is 1α-hydroxylase, and the target disease is Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. The specific mechanistic pathway is that 1α-hydroxylase is a key enzyme in the synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25(OH)2D3), which is the active form of vitamin D. The specific biological process is that mutations in the gene encoding 1α-hydroxylase result in reduced activity of the enzyme, leading to decreased levels of 1,25(OH)2D3 in the blood. This can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

We hypothesize that APIP is a causative gene for Hereditary multiple exostoses 1. APIP is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of 2-aminobutyric acid to 2-oxobutyric acid and the conversion of 2-oxobutyric acid to acetoin. The accumulation of 2-oxobutyric acid and acetoin in Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 patients may lead to the formation of exostoses. To test this hypothesis, we can measure the levels of 2-oxobutyric acid and acetoin in the blood of Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 patients and healthy controls. If the levels of 2-oxobutyric acid and acetoin are significantly higher in Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 patients than in healthy controls, it would confirm our hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ACP1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of toxic intermediates of the fatty acid beta-oxidation pathway, which in turn causes Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2. Specifically, we propose that ACP1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of 3-ketoacyl-CoA intermediates, which are toxic to mitochondria and cause oxidative stress. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that ACP1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of 3-ketoacyl-CoA intermediates in other diseases, and that these intermediates are known to be toxic to mitochondria. To test this hypothesis, we predict that measuring the levels of 3-ketoacyl-CoA intermediates in the blood or urine of patients with Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2 will reveal an increase in these intermediates compared to healthy controls. This would provide evidence that ACP1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of 3-ketoacyl-CoA intermediates in Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2.

We hypothesize that IP6K3 is a causative gene for sarcosinemia. IP6K3 is a kinase that phosphorylates inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) to produce inositol heptakisphosphate (IP7). IP6K3 is a member of the inositol polyphosphate kinase family, which is involved in the metabolism of phosphoinositides. IP6K3 is expressed in the liver, kidney, and brain. IP6K3 is a potential causative gene for sarcosinemia because it is involved in the metabolism of phosphoinositides, which are important for the transport of amino acids. IP6K3 is also involved in the metabolism of phosphatidylinositol, which is important for the transport of glucose. Therefore, mutations in IP6K3 may lead to the accumulation of amino acids and glucose in the blood, which is a characteristic of sarcosinemia.

We hypothesize that CAMKMT (calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase methylthiotransferase) is the enzyme responsible for the methylation of thiocysteine to methionine in the mitochondrial matrix. This enzyme is responsible for the methylation of thiocysteine to methionine in the mitochondrial matrix. The methylation of thiocysteine to methionine is a critical step in the mitochondrial methionine salvage pathway. The methionine salvage pathway is essential for the synthesis of methionine, which is required for the synthesis of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the primary methyl donor in the cell. SAM is required for the methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids. The methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids is essential for normal cellular function. The methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids is disrupted in Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata 2 (RCDP2). RCDP2 is a genetic disorder characterized by shortened limbs, intellectual disability, and seizures. The disruption of the methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids in RCDP2 is caused by a mutation in the CAMKMT gene. The mutation in the CAMKMT gene results in a loss of CAMKMT enzyme activity, which leads to a disruption of the methionine salvage pathway. The disruption of the methionine salvage pathway in RCDP2 results in a decrease in SAM levels, which leads to a global hypomethylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids. The global hypomethylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids in RCDP2 is the cause of the disease.

We hypothesize that ATP5MC1, a subunit of the mitochondrial ATP synthase, is a key enzyme in the pathogenesis of Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 2 (MTDPS2). Mitochondrial ATP synthase is a proton pump that generates ATP from ADP and phosphate. ATP5MC1 is a subunit of the c-ring of the F0F1 ATP synthase, which is the proton pumping component of the enzyme. ATP5MC1 is essential for the assembly of the c-ring and the formation of a functional ATP synthase.

We hypothesize that PIP4K2A is a causative gene for Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 (HME1). PIP4K2A encodes a kinase that phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PIP4) to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2). PIP4K2A is a member of the phosphatidylinositol kinase family, which is involved in the regulation of cell growth and proliferation. PIP4K2A is highly expressed in the growth plate, a cartilage layer at the ends of long bones. The growth plate is responsible for the elongation of the bone through the proliferation and differentiation of chondrocytes. The loss of PIP4K2A function may lead to abnormal chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, resulting in the formation of exostoses. The loss of PIP4K2A function may also affect the regulation of cell growth and proliferation, leading to abnormal bone development.

We hypothesize that AMD1 deficiency leads to Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency through a feedback mechanism. AMD1 is a cysteine biosynthesis enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to cysteine. Cystathionine beta-synthase is also involved in cysteine biosynthesis, but through a different pathway. If AMD1 is deficient, the buildup of homocysteine would lead to a feedback inhibition of cystathionine beta-synthase, resulting in a deficiency of cysteine. This would cause a deficiency of glutathione, which is essential for detoxifying reactive oxygen species. The accumulation of reactive oxygen species could lead to oxidative stress and damage to cells, tissues, and organs. This could result in the symptoms of Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, such as seizures, developmental delay, and intellectual disability.

We hypothesize that mutations in the MOCS2 gene, which encodes the enzyme cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS), lead to Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 16 (PCH16) by disrupting the methionine salvage pathway. Specifically, we propose that CBS mutations impair the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine, leading to a buildup of homocysteine and a subsequent depletion of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). This would impair the methylation of DNA and histones, leading to abnormal gene expression and cellular proliferation.

We hypothesize that TH, a mitochondrial enzyme involved in the synthesis of thiamine, is a causative gene for congenital disorder of glycosylation 1P (CDGP). CDGP is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the deficiency of N-glycosylated proteins. TH catalyzes the conversion of thiamine monophosphate (TMP) to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active form of thiamine. TPP is an essential cofactor for several enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism, including pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH), and branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH). These enzymes are involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, which is the main pathway for the production of energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The TCA cycle also provides intermediates for the synthesis of amino acids, lipids, and nucleotides. Therefore, TH plays a crucial role in energy production and the synthesis of macromolecules. We predict that TH deficiency will lead to the accumulation of TCA cycle intermediates, which will result in the inhibition of PDH, KGDH, and BCKDH. This inhibition will lead to the accumulation of amino acids, lipids, and nucleotides, which will result in the deficiency of N-glycosylated proteins. To confirm this hypothesis, we will measure the activity of PDH, KGDH, and BCKDH in TH-deficient mice and patients with CDGP.

We hypothesize that MLYCD deficiency in Schwann cells leads to a buildup of toxic metabolites, such as 3-methyl-2-oxovaleric acid, which causes axonal degeneration in peripheral nerves. This would explain the pathology of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2W.

We hypothesize that mutations in the gene encoding inositol 1-phosphate 4-kinase (IPMK) cause Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EVP4) by disrupting the conversion of inositol 1-phosphate (IP1) to inositol 4-phosphate (IP4). This would lead to a reduction in IP4 levels, which is essential for the synthesis of phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs) and phosphatidylinositol phosphate kinases (PIPKs). PIPs and PIPKs are involved in the regulation of cellular processes such as cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation.

We hypothesize that the familial erythrocytosis (FE) phenotype is caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the riboflavin kinase (RFK) enzyme. RFK is a key enzyme in the flavin biosynthesis pathway, which is essential for the production of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN). FAD and FMN are cofactors for a variety of enzymes, including those involved in energy metabolism and antioxidant defense. The FE phenotype is characterized by increased red blood cell mass, which can lead to an enlarged spleen and liver. We propose that a mutation in the RFK gene leads to a decrease in the activity of the enzyme, resulting in a deficiency of FAD and FMN. This deficiency can lead to an increase in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can damage red blood cells and lead to their increased production. This hypothesis can be tested by sequencing the RFK gene in patients with the FE phenotype and comparing it to the sequence in healthy individuals. If a mutation is found in the RFK gene, it can be tested by expressing the mutant RFK enzyme in vitro and measuring its activity. If the mutant enzyme has decreased activity, it would confirm the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that MAP2K1 is a causal factor in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2W. MAP2K1 is a dual-specificity mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase that activates p38 and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) mitogen-activated protein kinases. We propose that MAP2K1 is a causal factor in CMT2W because it is a kinase for the transcription factor c-Jun, which is a causal factor in CMT2W. We predict that CMT2W patients will have increased levels of c-Jun phosphorylation at residue Ser63, which is a known phosphorylation site for MAP2K1. This prediction can be tested by comparing c-Jun phosphorylation at residue Ser63 in CMT2W patients to control subjects.

We hypothesize that ACAA1 is a key regulator of chondrosarcoma cell proliferation and survival. ACAA1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the final step of β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, converting acyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and fatty acids. In chondrosarcoma cells, ACAA1 is overexpressed and localized to the cytosol, where it can convert acyl-CoAs to acetyl-CoA and acetate. This acetate is then converted to acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA synthetase (ACCS), which is also overexpressed in chondrosarcoma cells. The resulting acetyl-CoA is then used to generate citrate via citrate synthase, which can then be exported to the cytosol via the mitochondrial citrate transporter (SLC13A5). In the cytosol, citrate is converted to oxaloacetate by ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY), which is also overexpressed in chondrosarcoma cells. Oxaloacetate is then used in the synthesis of aspartate via aspartate aminotransferase (GOT1), which is also overexpressed in chondrosarcoma cells. Aspartate is then used in the synthesis of nucleotides and amino acids, which are required for chondrosarcoma cell proliferation and survival.

We hypothesize that HSD17B14 is a key enzyme in the metabolic pathway leading to the production of the Brugada syndrome 2 (BrS2) electrocardiogram (ECG) pattern. HSD17B14 is a steroid hydroxylase that converts 5α-pregnane-3,20-dione (5α-Pregnane-3,20-dione) to 5α-pregnan-3α-ol-20-one (5α-Pregnan-3α-ol-20-one). 5α-Pregnane-3,20-dione is a steroid hormone that is a metabolite of progesterone and is involved in the production of the BrS2 ECG pattern. The BrS2 ECG pattern is characterized by a coved-type ST segment elevation in the right precordial leads and a negative T wave in lead V2. This ECG pattern is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. We predict that inhibition of HSD17B14 will result in a decrease in the production of 5α-Pregnan-3α-ol-20-one and a decrease in the incidence of the BrS2 ECG pattern. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of 5α-Pregnan-3α-ol-20-one in patients with the BrS2 ECG pattern before and after treatment with an HSD17B14 inhibitor.

terminal_shown: Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HSD17B14, a fucose metabolizing enzyme, is a causative gene for congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2 (CDG-fucosylation). HSD17B14 catalyzes the conversion of D-mannose-1-phosphate to D-fructose-6-phosphate, which is a precursor for fucose synthesis. Loss of HSD17B14 activity leads to a reduction in fucosylation of glycoproteins, which is the hallmark of CDG-fucosylation. To test this hypothesis, we propose to measure the activity of HSD17B14 in patient fibroblasts and compare it to control fibroblasts. We predict that the activity of HSD17B14 will be reduced in patient fibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts.

We hypothesize that PIK3C3 deficiency leads to Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 1. PIK3C3 is a phosphatidylinositol kinase that converts phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate, which is a key step in the insulin signaling pathway. Insulin signaling is required for the synthesis of coenzyme Q10 in the mitochondria. Therefore, we predict that patients with PIK3C3 deficiency will have lower levels of coenzyme Q10 in their mitochondria. This can be tested by measuring the levels of coenzyme Q10 in the mitochondria of patients with PIK3C3 deficiency compared to healthy controls.

terminal_shown: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GRB2, a protein tyrosine kinase, is a causal factor in the development of Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC). GRB2 is known to be involved in the activation of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK pathway, which is a major signaling pathway involved in cell proliferation and differentiation. HLRCC is caused by mutations in the FH gene, which encodes the fumarate hydratase enzyme. This enzyme is involved in the citric acid cycle and is responsible for the conversion of fumarate to malate. In the absence of functional fumarate hydratase, fumarate accumulates and acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme hydroxylase, which is involved in the production of the signaling molecule p53. The accumulation of fumarate leads to the inactivation of p53, which in turn leads to the activation of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK pathway. GRB2 is known to be involved in the activation of this pathway, so we hypothese that it is a causal factor in the development of HLRCC.

terminal_shown: Calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that RRM2B is a key regulator of the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity in the calvaria, and that its dysregulation leads to calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. RRM2B is a key regulator of ribonucleotide reductase, which catalyzes the reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, the building blocks of DNA. RRM2B is highly expressed in proliferating cells, including osteoblasts, and is downregulated during differentiation. We propose that RRM2B dysregulation leads to aberrant osteoblast proliferation and inhibits osteoblast differentiation, resulting in a failure to maintain the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity. This imbalance leads to the formation of calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. To test this hypothesis, we predict that RRM2B expression is increased in calvarial osteoblasts of patients with calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, and that this increase is associated with an increase in osteoblast proliferation and a decrease in osteoblast differentiation.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A10
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that FBP1 deficiency leads to muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A10 (MDDGA10) due to impaired glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. FBP1 is a key enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) that catalyzes the conversion of F6P to FBP1. FBP1 deficiency leads to a decrease in the N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) levels, which are essential for the glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. The glycosylation of α-dystroglycan is crucial for its binding to laminin, a component of the extracellular matrix. The lack of binding of α-dystroglycan to laminin leads to the destabilization of the muscle membrane and the development of muscular dystrophy. The decrease in GlcNAc levels also affects the glycosylation of other proteins, such as β-dystroglycan, perlecan, and agrin, which are important for the proper functioning of the brain and eye. The decrease in the glycosylation of these proteins leads to the development of brain and eye anomalies.

We hypothesize that KYAT3, a key enzyme in the kynurenine pathway, is involved in the pathogenesis of Anterior Segment Dysgenesis 6 (ASD6). KYAT3 catalyzes the conversion of kynurenine to anthranilate, a precursor for the synthesis of NAD+. NAD+ is a cofactor for sirtuin deacetylases, which regulate the expression of genes involved in cellular differentiation and apoptosis. We predict that mutations in KYAT3 will lead to decreased NAD+ levels, resulting in altered sirtuin activity and aberrant gene expression in the developing eye. This will manifest as ASD6, a congenital eye disease characterized by iris hypoplasia, corectopia, and other iris and lens abnormalities. To test this hypothesis, we will measure NAD+ levels in ASD6 patients with KYAT3 mutations and compare them to NAD+ levels in ASD6 patients without KYAT3 mutations and in healthy controls.

We hypothesize that CDKN2A is a causative gene for Trichothiodystrophy 7, non-photosensitive. CDKN2A encodes a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, p16INK4A, which is a tumor suppressor protein. The p16INK4A protein binds to cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and cyclin-dependent kinase 6 (CDK6) to inhibit the cell cycle. CDKN2A is a tumor suppressor gene that is frequently inactivated in various cancers. CDKN2A is located on chromosome 9p21, which is a region of the genome that is frequently deleted in cancer. The loss of CDKN2A expression in cancer cells leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumorigenesis.

We hypothesize that mutations in ADPGK, a glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of ADP-glucose to ADP-glucose pyrophosphate, are associated with Lethal congenital contracture syndrome 2. ADPGK is a key enzyme in the glycolytic pathway and its activity is essential for the production of ATP. Mutations in ADPGK may lead to a decrease in ATP production, which is required for muscle contraction. This could result in muscle weakness and contractures, which are the hallmark features of Lethal congenital contracture syndrome 2.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GOT1L1 is a causative gene for Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2. GOT1L1 encodes the mitochondrial isoform of glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (GOT1), which catalyzes the reversible conversion of aspartate to oxaloacetate and alanine to glutamate. GOT1L1 is localized to the mitochondrial matrix and is a component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), which is a key regulator of mitochondrial metabolism. PDC is a multi-enzyme complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, which is then used in the citric acid cycle to produce ATP. The activity of PDC is regulated by reversible phosphorylation of the E1α subunit, which is catalyzed by PDC phosphorylase (PDK) and PDC dephosphorylase (PDP). We hypothesize that GOT1L1 is a causative gene for Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2 because mutations in GOT1L1 may disrupt the activity of PDC, leading to a decrease in mitochondrial metabolism and ATP production. This could result in mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired energy production, which are hallmark features of Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2.

We hypothesize that PTDSS1 is a causative gene for sialuria. PTDSS1 encodes a protein that is involved in the biosynthesis of sialic acid, a type of sugar found in glycoproteins and glycolipids. Sialic acid is an important component of the cell surface and plays a crucial role in cell-cell interactions, immune responses, and cancer metastasis. The absence of sialic acid in sialuria patients leads to the accumulation of gangliosides, which are toxic to the body. PTDSS1 is a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of sialic acid and its absence can lead to sialuria. We predict that patients with sialuria will have a mutation in the PTDSS1 gene, which will be confirmed by sequencing the gene.

We hypothesize that ASNS deficiency leads to elevated levels of asparagine in the blood, which in turn leads to the inhibition of the enzyme succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase (SCOT). This inhibition would lead to a buildup of succinyl-CoA, which is toxic to cells. To test this hypothesis, we would measure the levels of asparagine and succinyl-CoA in the blood of patients with SCOT deficiency and compare them to healthy controls. If our hypothesis is correct, we would expect to see higher levels of asparagine and succinyl-CoA in the blood of patients with SCOT deficiency.

We hypothesize that PRUNE1 is a key enzyme in the metabolism of pulmonary surfactant phospholipids. In particular, we propose that PRUNE1 is a phospholipase A2 (PLA2) that specifically cleaves the sn-2 acyl chain of pulmonary surfactant phospholipids. This would be a novel function for a PLA2, as all known PLA2s cleave the sn-1 acyl chain. This would explain the pathogenesis of Pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3, which is characterized by abnormal surfactant phospholipid metabolism.

We hypothesize that mutations in the AMY1A gene, which encodes the pancreatic amylase enzyme, may be associated with pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 12 (PCH12). PCH12 is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and intellectual disability. Amylase is a digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into simple sugars in the small intestine. It is also expressed in the brain, where it has been shown to play a role in neurogenesis and neuronal migration during development. Mutations in the AMY1A gene have been associated with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. We predict that mutations in AMY1A may lead to PCH12 through disruption of amylase function in the brain, resulting in abnormal neurogenesis and neuronal migration during development. This could be tested by examining the expression and function of amylase in the brains of individuals with PCH12 and comparing it to controls.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PLPP1 deficiency leads to Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8. PLPP1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylation of lipoyl groups to lipoyl-CoA, which is essential for the assembly of mitochondrial complex I. We predict that PLPP1 deficiency leads to a reduction in the activity of mitochondrial complex I, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. This would lead to mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular damage, which could manifest as Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8. To test this hypothesis, we would measure the activity of mitochondrial complex I and ROS production in patient-derived cells and tissues. A decrease in mitochondrial complex I activity and an increase in ROS production would confirm our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that MGAM, a small intestinal maltase, is a causative factor in Familial porphyria cutanea tarda. MGAM is a member of the alpha-glucosidase family of enzymes, which hydrolyzes the terminal alpha-glucosidic linkages of oligosaccharides and glycogen. MGAM is expressed in the small intestine and is involved in the digestion of starch.

terminal_shown: Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that MSH2, a DNA mismatch repair protein, is the source enzyme for Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 1. MSH2 is a DNA mismatch repair protein that interacts with MSH6 to form a heterodimer. This heterodimer is responsible for the recognition of mismatched bases in DNA. MSH2/MSH6 recognizes the mismatched base and recruits the endonuclease MLH1/PMS2 to the site of the mismatch. This leads to the excision of the mismatched base and the insertion of the correct nucleotide.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in ASRGL1 cause Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay by disrupting the function of the enzyme aspartyl-tRNA synthetase. This enzyme is responsible for charging tRNA with aspartic acid, an essential amino acid. Aspartic acid is required for the synthesis of proteins, which are the building blocks of cells. If the enzyme is not functioning properly, it can lead to a buildup of uncharged tRNA, which can interfere with protein synthesis. This can cause cells to malfunction and eventually lead to disease.

We hypothesize that Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase 1 (GPLD1) is a key regulator of iron homeostasis in the brain. GPLD1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, producing NADH in the process. In the brain, GPLD1 is expressed in neurons and astrocytes, and its activity is regulated by iron levels. When iron levels are low, GPLD1 activity is inhibited, leading to a decrease in NADH production. This, in turn, leads to a decrease in the activity of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, which reduces the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). This is important because ROS are known to cause oxidative damage to proteins, lipids, and DNA, which can lead to neurodegeneration. We predict that in Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 6 patients, GPLD1 activity will be decreased in the brain, leading to increased ROS production and oxidative damage. This can be tested by measuring GPLD1 activity in post-mortem brain tissue from Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 6 patients and comparing it to activity in post-mortem brain tissue from healthy controls.

We hypothesize that PLOD1, an enzyme involved in the hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen, is a causative gene for LCA14. PLOD1 is expressed in the retina and is involved in the formation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the retina. The ECM is a critical component of the retina, providing structural support and regulating cell-cell interactions. Mutations in PLOD1 may disrupt the formation of the ECM in the retina, leading to abnormal cell-cell interactions and impaired retinal function. This could manifest as the symptoms of LCA14, including impaired vision and blindness.

We hypothesize that EHMT2 is a causative gene for Galactosemia 4. EHMT2 encodes a histone methyltransferase that catalyzes the mono- and di-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me1 and H3K9me2). In the presence of galactose, EHMT2 is recruited to the promoter region of the GALT gene, which encodes galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the Leloir pathway of galactose metabolism. The recruitment of EHMT2 to the GALT promoter results in the repression of GALT gene expression, leading to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and the subsequent development of Galactosemia 4.

We hypothesize that LPCAT3 is a key enzyme in the pathogenesis of cholesteryl ester storage disease (CESD). LPCAT3 is a phospholipid acyltransferase that catalyzes the acylation of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) with arachidonic acid (AA) to produce phosphatidylcholine (PC) and AA. In CESD, LPCAT3 is upregulated in the liver and downregulated in the kidney. This imbalance leads to the accumulation of LPC in the liver and a deficiency of LPC in the kidney. The accumulation of LPC in the liver leads to the formation of cholesteryl esters, which are stored in the liver. The deficiency of LPC in the kidney leads to the formation of oxidized phospholipids, which are toxic to the kidney. We predict that inhibiting LPCAT3 in the liver will reduce the formation of cholesteryl esters and improve kidney function in CESD patients.

We hypothesize that MAPK8 is a causative gene for dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency. MAPK8 is a member of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family, which plays a crucial role in cellular signaling. MAPK8 is involved in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. It is also involved in the regulation of immune responses and inflammation. Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD) is an enzyme that is involved in the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). DLD deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that is characterized by the accumulation of BCAAs in the blood and tissues. The accumulation of BCAAs can lead to various symptoms, including intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and seizures. We predict that MAPK8 is a causative gene for dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency. This hypothesis can be tested by sequencing the MAPK8 gene in patients with dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency and analyzing the expression of MAPK8 in cells and tissues of these patients.

We hypothesize that CISD1 is a mitochondrial protein that transports electrons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space. Mutations in CISD1 lead to a decrease in the activity of the respiratory chain complexes, resulting in a reduction in the production of ATP. This leads to a decrease in the energy available for the transport of potassium ions across the cell membrane, which is necessary for the proper functioning of the auditory hair cells. This results in hearing loss.

We hypothesize that GATM deficiency in intestinal epithelial cells leads to increased levels of 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxodG) in the gut, which in turn causes inflammatory bowel disease 13 (IBD13). GATM is a DNA glycosylase that removes 8-oxodG from DNA, and its deficiency leads to accumulation of 8-oxodG in DNA. 8-oxodG is a major product of DNA oxidation, and its accumulation in DNA leads to DNA damage and mutations. 8-oxodG is also present in RNA, and its accumulation in RNA leads to protein mistranslation and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS are known to cause inflammation and oxidative stress, which are hallmarks of IBD13. Therefore, we predict that GATM deficiency in intestinal epithelial cells will lead to increased levels of 8-oxodG in DNA and RNA, which in turn will cause inflammation and oxidative stress in the gut, leading to IBD13. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of 8-oxodG in DNA and RNA in intestinal epithelial cells of GATM-deficient mice and comparing them to the levels in intestinal epithelial cells of wild-type mice.

We hypothesize that PNPLA6 deficiency in humans leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters in the liver, which is then secreted into the bloodstream. This results in the formation of xanthomas in tendons and the brain, as well as the development of cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

We hypothesize that PTDSS2 is a causative gene for Hypercholanemia, familial 3. PTDSS2 encodes a protein that is involved in the biosynthesis of bile acids. Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver and secreted into the intestine, where they emulsify dietary lipids and facilitate their absorption. Bile acids are also reabsorbed from the intestine and transported back to the liver. The biosynthesis of bile acids is a complex process that involves several enzymes and is tightly regulated to maintain homeostasis. PTDSS2 is involved in the first step of this process, catalyzing the conversion of cholesterol to 7α-OHC. We hypothesize that a loss of function mutation in PTDSS2 leads to a decrease in the production of 7α-OHC, resulting in a reduction in the synthesis of bile acids. This would lead to an accumulation of cholesterol in the liver and intestine, which could cause liver damage and diarrhea. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of 7α-OHC in patients with Hypercholanemia, familial 3 and comparing them to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that CYP8B1 is a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC), a precursor to cholesterol. CYP8B1 is a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily of enzymes, which are involved in the metabolism of steroid hormones, bile acids, and other lipids. 7-DHC is a precursor to cholesterol, which is a component of cell membranes and plays a critical role in cell signaling. Cholesterol is also a precursor to bile acids, which are involved in the digestion and absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins.

We hypothesize that ASMT is the source enzyme for Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. ASMT catalyzes the final step in the methylation of vitamin D, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3. This is the active form of vitamin D, which is essential for bone growth and development. We propose that a mutation in the ASMT gene leads to a decrease in the activity of the enzyme, resulting in a deficiency of active vitamin D. This deficiency can lead to rickets, a condition characterized by weak and soft bones. To test this hypothesis, we would measure the activity of ASMT in patients with Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A and compare it to healthy controls. We would also measure the levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 in the patients and compare them to healthy controls. We would expect to see a decrease in the activity of ASMT and a decrease in the levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 in patients with Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A.

We hypothesize that LTA4H deficiency in osteoclasts leads to increased bone density due to impaired osteoclast differentiation and function. LTA4H catalyzes the conversion of leukotriene A4 (LTA4) to LTA4 hydroxylase (LTA4H), a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils. LTA4H is expressed in osteoclasts and is involved in osteoclast differentiation and function. LTA4H deficiency in osteoclasts may lead to impaired osteoclast differentiation and function, resulting in increased bone density. To test this hypothesis, we will measure the expression of LTA4H in osteoclasts from patients with osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive 3 and compare it to osteoclasts from healthy controls. We will also measure the bone density of patients with osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive 3 and compare it to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that PCYT1A deficiency leads to Adenylosuccinase deficiency. PCYT1A is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of cytosine 5'-diphosphocholine (CDP-choline) to choline. Choline is a precursor for the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine, a major component of cell membranes. PCYT1A deficiency leads to a decrease in choline levels, which can result in the accumulation of adenosine and adenosine monophosphate (AMP). Adenosine and AMP are substrates for adenylosuccinate synthase, which converts them to adenylosuccinate. Adenylosuccinate is then converted to inosine monophosphate (IMP) by adenylosuccinase. Deficiency of adenylosuccinase leads to the accumulation of adenylosuccinate, which can result in the development of Adenylosuccinase deficiency.

We hypothesize that GALC deficiency leads to the accumulation of galactosylceramide in the retina, which in turn leads to the degeneration of photoreceptors and the development of retinitis pigmentosa. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that GALC deficiency is associated with the accumulation of galactosylceramide in the brain, which leads to Krabbe's disease. To test this hypothesis, we propose to measure the levels of galactosylceramide in the retinas of patients with retinitis pigmentosa and compare them to healthy controls. We also propose to measure the levels of galactosylceramide in the retinas of animal models of retinitis pigmentosa and compare them to healthy controls. We expect to find higher levels of galactosylceramide in the retinas of patients and animal models of retinitis pigmentosa compared to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that UQCRQ is a modifier of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency. UQCRQ is a subunit of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III, which is involved in the electron transport chain. The electron transport chain is a series of protein complexes that transfer electrons from NADH and FADH2 to oxygen, generating a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This proton gradient is used to generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. UQCRQ is a subunit of complex III that binds ubiquinone, which is the electron acceptor for complex III. UQCRQ is a potential modifier of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency because it is involved in the electron transport chain, which is a major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS are produced as byproducts of the electron transport chain and can cause oxidative damage to cells. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency is a disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, and oxidative stress is a major contributor to the pathogenesis of the disease. Therefore, we predict that patients with Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency will have higher levels of ROS than controls. This can be tested by measuring the levels of ROS in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency and controls using flow cytometry.

terminal_shown: Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that XDH is a causative factor in the development of polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts. XDH is a key enzyme in the purine metabolism pathway, which is known to be involved in the development of cysts in the liver and kidneys. XDH catalyzes the oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine and then to uric acid, which is the final product of purine metabolism. The accumulation of uric acid in the bloodstream can lead to the formation of uric acid crystals, which can cause inflammation and tissue damage. This inflammation and tissue damage can contribute to the development of cysts in the liver and kidneys.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that COQ5 deficiency leads to a reduction in coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) levels, which in turn causes a decrease in ATP production and an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. This leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, which can cause cellular damage and dysfunction. This can result in neurodegeneration and neurodevelopmental disorders, including microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures.

We hypothesize that CDKN1A is a causative gene for 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency. CDKN1A encodes p21, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that regulates cell cycle progression. Inhibition of p21 by cyclin-dependent kinases is mediated by phosphorylation of p21 at serine 146. Phosphorylation of p21 at serine 146 is catalyzed by CDK1, CDK2, and CDK4. We predict that mutations in CDKN1A that disrupt the phosphorylation of p21 at serine 146 will result in increased p21 activity, leading to cell cycle arrest and decreased cell proliferation. This will result in decreased production of 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase, leading to 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency. This hypothesis can be tested by identifying mutations in CDKN1A that disrupt phosphorylation of p21 at serine 146 in patients with 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B4GALT1 is a causative gene for Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4. B4GALT1 is a Golgi-localized enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the biosynthesis of galactosylceramide, a major component of the glycosphingolipid class of lipids. Glycosphingolipids are essential for the assembly of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, and their deficiency has been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction. We predict that B4GALT1 deficiency leads to a reduction in the levels of galactosylceramide and other glycosphingolipids, resulting in impaired assembly of mitochondrial complex II and leading to the clinical features of Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of galactosylceramide and other glycosphingolipids in patients with Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4 and in animal models of B4GALT1 deficiency.

We hypothesize that Laurence-Moon syndrome is caused by a deficiency in the GALK1 enzyme, which catalyzes the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate in the Leloir pathway of galactose metabolism. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in cells, resulting in the inhibition of glycolysis and the activation of the pentose phosphate pathway. This, in turn, leads to the production of reactive oxygen species and oxidative stress, which can cause cellular damage and dysfunction. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that GALK1 deficiency has been associated with other diseases involving oxidative stress, such as diabetes and cancer.

We hypothesize that NUS1 is a mechanistic driver of inflammatory bowel disease 13 (IBD13). NUS1 is a nucleolar protein that is involved in ribosome biogenesis and is essential for cell proliferation. It has been shown to be overexpressed in various cancers and is associated with poor prognosis. NUS1 is also involved in the regulation of the immune response through its role in ribosome biogenesis. In particular, it has been shown to be involved in the regulation of the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

We hypothesize that Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase (SQR) deficiency is caused by a disruption of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) due to the accumulation of sulfide (H2S) in the mitochondrial matrix. SQR is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of sulfide to sulfate, using quinone as an electron acceptor. In SQR deficiency, sulfide accumulates in the mitochondrial matrix, where it can react with oxygen to form superoxide. Superoxide can then be converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by superoxide dismutase (SOD), or it can react with other electron acceptors to form other reactive oxygen species (ROS). The accumulation of ROS can lead to oxidative stress and damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA. This can disrupt the function of the ETC, leading to a vicious cycle of further ROS production and mitochondrial damage.

We hypothesize that CH25H is a causative gene for Perrault syndrome 2. CH25H is a cytochrome P450 enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, a precursor of steroid hormones. Pregnenolone is also a substrate for the synthesis of neurosteroids, which are steroid hormones that act as allosteric modulators of neurotransmitter receptors. Neurosteroids have been shown to modulate the activity of GABA receptors, which are the target of mutations in Perrault syndrome 1. We predict that mutations in CH25H will lead to altered levels of neurosteroids, which will in turn affect the activity of GABA receptors. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of neurosteroids in patients with Perrault syndrome 2 and by examining the effects of CH25H mutations on the activity of GABA receptors in vitro.

We hypothesize that N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency is caused by a mechanistic connection between the source enzyme AGA and the target disease. Specifically, we propose that the accumulation of N-acetylglutamate (NAG) in N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency is due to a feedback inhibition of AGA by NAG. This would result in a decrease in the production of N-acetylglutamate, which is an essential cofactor for the urea cycle. This decrease in N-acetylglutamate would lead to the accumulation of other urea cycle intermediates, such as citrulline and arginine, which are known to cause symptoms of N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency.

terminal_shown: Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that DEGS2 is a causative gene for Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures. DEGS2 encodes a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. We propose that mutations in DEGS2 lead to a decrease in the activity of this enzyme, resulting in a buildup of dihydroxyacetone phosphate. This, in turn, leads to an increase in the activity of the oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, resulting in an increase in the production of NADPH. NADPH is a cofactor for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide to water, and an increase in its levels would lead to a decrease in the levels of hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species that is known to cause oxidative damage to proteins, lipids, and DNA. We predict that mutations in DEGS2 will lead to a decrease in the levels of hydrogen peroxide, resulting in a decrease in oxidative damage to proteins, lipids, and DNA. This would lead to a decrease in the severity of the symptoms of Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of hydrogen peroxide in cells with and without mutations in DEGS2.

We hypothesize that mutations in SOAT1, a cholesterol-esterifying enzyme, lead to Hypotrichosis 4. SOAT1 is a cholesterol-esterifying enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an acyl group from an acyl-CoA to a hydroxyl group of a sterol, resulting in the formation of a sterol ester. SOAT1 is expressed in the liver, kidney, and small intestine, and is involved in the metabolism of cholesterol and bile acids. SOAT1 is also expressed in the hair follicle, where it is involved in the formation of sebaceous glands. Sebaceous glands are specialized glands that produce sebum, a mixture of lipids that lubricate and waterproof the skin and hair. Sebaceous glands are composed of sebaceous ducts, sebaceous lobules, and sebaceous gland orifices. The sebaceous gland orifices open onto the skin surface through hair follicles.

We hypothesize that NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) iron-sulfur protein 3 (NDUFS3) is a key regulator of collagen synthesis in the Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1 (EDS-MC) pathogenesis. NDUFS3 is a subunit of the mitochondrial complex I, which is a major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the cell. ROS are known to induce collagen synthesis in fibroblasts, and NDUFS3 deficiency may lead to increased ROS production. We predict that fibroblasts derived from EDS-MC patients will have increased collagen synthesis compared to fibroblasts from healthy controls. This prediction can be tested by measuring collagen synthesis in fibroblasts derived from EDS-MC patients and healthy controls.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that MAN2A2 deficiency leads to the accumulation of mannosylated glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), causing ER stress and the unfolded protein response (UPR). This results in the activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is known to be involved in neurodevelopmental disorders. The accumulation of mannosylated glycoproteins in the ER can be confirmed by mass spectrometry, and the activation of the JNK pathway can be confirmed by Western blot analysis of phosphorylated c-Jun. The accumulation of mannosylated glycoproteins in the ER can be caused by the inhibition of MAN2A2 activity using small molecule inhibitors, which would lead to the activation of the JNK pathway. The activation of the JNK pathway can be inhibited by the use of JNK inhibitors, which would prevent the development of the neurodevelopmental disorder.

We hypothesize that the loss of ARSA enzyme activity in Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency leads to a decrease in the production of 2-hydroxy-3-methylvalerate (HMV), which is a precursor for the synthesis of the neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA). This decrease in GABA levels would lead to an increase in the levels of glutamate, which is an excitatory neurotransmitter. This increase in glutamate levels would lead to excitotoxicity, which is a known cause of neuronal damage. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of HMV and GABA in the brains of patients with Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency and comparing them to healthy controls. If the levels of HMV and GABA are lower in patients with Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency, then this would support the hypothesis. If the levels of HMV and GABA are similar in patients with Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency and healthy controls, then this would disprove the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that PGAP2, a Golgi-localized phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase, is a causative gene for Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy (SCDD). PGAP2 is a Golgi-localized phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase that catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidic acid to phosphatidylglycerophosphate, a precursor of phosphatidylinositol. Phosphatidylinositol is a precursor of inositol phospholipids, which are essential for cellular signaling and metabolism. Inositol phospholipids are also involved in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, which is essential for cellular motility and adhesion. SCDD is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia and cone-rod dystrophy. The disease is caused by mutations in the PGAP2 gene, which is expressed in the brain, kidney, and retina. The retina is particularly affected in SCDD, leading to retinal degeneration and blindness. The role of PGAP2 in the retina is not well understood. We hypothesize that PGAP2 is involved in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in the retina, which is essential for photoreceptor cell morphogenesis and maintenance. We predict that loss of PGAP2 function in the retina will lead to actin cytoskeleton disorganization and photoreceptor cell degeneration. This hypothesis can be tested by examining the actin cytoskeleton in PGAP2-deficient retinal cells and investigating the effects of PGAP2 deficiency on photoreceptor cell morphogenesis and maintenance.

We hypothesize that CYP4F8 is a key enzyme in the metabolic pathway leading to the development of Bachmann-Büpp syndrome. CYP4F8 is a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily of enzymes, which are responsible for the metabolism of a wide variety of endogenous and exogenous compounds. CYP4F8 is expressed in the liver and is involved in the metabolism of cholesterol and steroid hormones.

terminal_shown: Developmental delay with short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and sparse hair 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CARNMT1 is a key regulator of the methionine cycle in humans. In the methionine cycle, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the primary methyl donor for methylation reactions in the cell. SAM is synthesized from methionine by SAM synthase, and is then used in methylation reactions. After these reactions, SAM is converted back to methionine by SAM decarboxylase. We hypothesize that CARNMT1 is a key regulator of this cycle, as it is a methyltransferase that catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from SAM to carnitine to form trimethyl-L-carnitine. If CARNMT1 is deficient, this would lead to a buildup of SAM and a decrease in methionine. This would result in a decrease in methylation reactions in the cell, leading to the developmental delay, short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and sparse hair phenotype seen in patients with mutations in CARNMT1.

We hypothesize that CARS2 deficiency in Trichothiodystrophy 9, non-photosensitive leads to a decrease in the production of cysteine, which is essential for the formation of disulfide bonds in keratin. This results in weakened keratin and fragile hair and nails.

We hypothesize that PPIP5K2 is a key regulator of the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway, which is known to be dysregulated in schizophrenia. Specifically, we propose that PPIP5K2 is a key regulator of the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway through its role in the synthesis of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3). These signaling molecules are known to be involved in the regulation of neuronal function, including synaptic transmission and plasticity. We predict that genetic variants in the PPIP5K2 gene will be associated with schizophrenia, and that changes in the expression or activity of PPIP5K2 will alter the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway and lead to changes in neuronal function. This hypothesis can be tested by examining the association of genetic variants in the PPIP5K2 gene with schizophrenia, and by examining the effects of changes in the expression or activity of PPIP5K2 on the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway and neuronal function.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and speech delay, with or without brain abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GALNS deficiency leads to the accumulation of sialylated glycoconjugates, which disrupts the function of the lysosomal compartment. This leads to the accumulation of autophagic vacuoles in neurons, which causes neurodegeneration and microcephaly.

We hypothesize that FAHD1 deficiency leads to phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency by disrupting the phosphoserine phosphatase pathway. FAHD1 is a phosphoserine aminotransferase that catalyzes the conversion of phosphoserine to phosphoserine phosphatase. Phosphoserine phosphatase is a key enzyme in the phosphoserine phosphatase pathway, which is essential for the synthesis of phosphoserine. If FAHD1 is deficient, phosphoserine aminotransferase activity is reduced, leading to a decrease in phosphoserine phosphatase activity and phosphoserine phosphatase pathway disruption. This would result in a deficiency of phosphoserine phosphatase, which is the enzyme that catalyzes the final step in the phosphoserine phosphatase pathway. This would lead to a deficiency in phosphoserine, which is an essential amino acid. A deficiency in phosphoserine can lead to a variety of health problems, including neurological and developmental disorders.

We hypothesize that the loss of function of CHDH enzyme in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1 is due to the accumulation of choline in the body. Choline is an essential nutrient that is converted to betaine by CHDH in the liver. Betaine is then converted to dimethylglycine (DMG) and excreted in urine. In the absence of CHDH activity, choline is not converted to betaine and DMG, and accumulates in the body. Choline accumulation has been shown to cause cellular dysfunction and apoptosis in vitro. We predict that the accumulation of choline in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1 will lead to cellular dysfunction and apoptosis in the body. This can be tested by measuring the levels of choline in the blood and urine of patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1 and comparing them to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that CDO1 deficiency leads to hyperoxaluria type 1 by disrupting the oxidation of catecholamines. CDO1 is a catecholamine dehydroxylase that catalyzes the oxidation of catecholamines to their corresponding quinones. The deficiency of CDO1 leads to the accumulation of catecholamines in the body, which can be oxidized to catechol quinones. Catechol quinones can be further oxidized to benzoquinones, which can be metabolized to oxalate. The accumulation of catecholamines and the increased production of oxalate can lead to hyperoxaluria type 1.

We hypothesize that PYCR2 is a causative gene for Glutaric aciduria 1 (GA1). GA1 is a recessive disorder caused by deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH), which converts glutaryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA. PYCR2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the final step of the pyrimidine biosynthesis pathway, converting dihydroorotate to orotate. In the absence of GCDH, glutaryl-CoA accumulates and inhibits PYCR2, leading to a secondary deficiency of orotate. Orotate is a precursor for pyrimidine biosynthesis, and its deficiency leads to a reduction in pyrimidine synthesis. Pyrimidines are essential building blocks for DNA and RNA synthesis, and their deficiency leads to cell death. Therefore, we predict that GA1 patients will have reduced pyrimidine levels in their urine.

We hypothesize that MPI deficiency in Usher syndrome 3B patients leads to the accumulation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) and its downstream metabolites, which in turn causes retinal degeneration. MPI catalyzes the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA and CO2, and its deficiency results in the accumulation of MMA and its downstream metabolites, including methylmalonic aciduria (MMAU), methylmalonic acidemia (MMA), and methylmalonic acid thioesterase (MATE). These metabolites are known to be toxic to the retina, causing retinal degeneration. To test this hypothesis, we propose to measure the levels of MMA and its downstream metabolites in the retina of Usher syndrome 3B patients and compare them to healthy controls. We expect to find higher levels of these metabolites in the retina of Usher syndrome 3B patients compared to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that GLUD1 deficiency leads to 5-oxoprolinase deficiency through a feedback inhibition mechanism. In the absence of GLUD1, the accumulation of 5-oxoprolinase leads to the inhibition of the downstream enzymes in the urea cycle, resulting in the accumulation of ammonia and other metabolic waste products. This feedback inhibition mechanism is a known regulatory process in metabolic pathways, and it has been observed in other metabolic disorders. To test this hypothesis, we predict that the expression of GLUD1 in patients with 5-oxoprolinase deficiency will be significantly lower than in healthy controls.

terminal_shown: Neuropathy, hereditary motor and sensory, 6C, with optic atrophy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that DHFR deficiency leads to elevated homocysteine levels, which in turn causes oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to neuronal damage and optic atrophy. This is supported by the fact that homocysteine is known to cause oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and that DHFR deficiency can lead to elevated homocysteine levels. To test this hypothesis, we would measure homocysteine levels in patients with Neuropathy, hereditary motor and sensory, 6C, with optic atrophy and compare them to controls. We would also measure oxidative stress and mitochondrial function in cells with DHFR deficiency and elevated homocysteine levels.

terminal_shown: Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that Acyl-CoA oxidase 1 (ACOX1) deficiency leads to Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy (LDDMN) through a mechanism involving peroxisomal dysfunction. ACOX1 is a peroxisomal enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). VLCFA metabolism is essential for myelin formation and maintenance, and peroxisomal dysfunction has been implicated in several neurological disorders. ACOX1 deficiency would lead to the accumulation of VLCFA-containing lipids in peroxisomes, which could impair peroxisomal function and myelin formation. This could result in the demyelination and axonal degeneration seen in LDDMN.

We hypothesize that CYP2B6 metabolism of the drug efavirenz (EFV) contributes to dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in patients with HIV. EFV is a commonly prescribed antiretroviral drug that is metabolized by CYP2B6. CYP2B6 is a member of the cytochrome P450 family of enzymes that metabolize a variety of endogenous compounds and xenobiotics. EFV is metabolized by CYP2B6 to its major metabolite, 8-hydroxyefavirenz (8-OH-EFV), which is a reactive electrophile. 8-OH-EFV can covalently bind to proteins, including cardiac myosin, to form stable adducts. These adducts may alter the structure and function of myosin, leading to impaired cardiac function and DCM. We predict that patients with HIV who are treated with EFV will have increased levels of 8-OH-EFV-protein adducts in their hearts compared to patients who are not treated with EFV. This can be tested by measuring the levels of 8-OH-EFV-protein adducts in heart tissue samples from patients with HIV who are treated with or not treated with EFV.

We hypothesize that PSAP is a key enzyme in the metabolic pathway leading to the development of Brugada syndrome 2. PSAP is a phosphatidylserine-specific phosphatase that catalyzes the dephosphorylation of phosphatidylserine (PS) to phosphatidic acid (PA). PSAP is highly expressed in the heart, and its expression is regulated by the sympathetic nervous system. PSAP is involved in the regulation of cardiac function, and its dysfunction has been implicated in the development of cardiac arrhythmias.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HSD11B1 is involved in the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14. HSD11B1 is a steroid dehydrogenase that catalyzes the interconversion of cortisol and cortisone. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone that regulates carbohydrate metabolism, and its dysregulation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophy. We predict that HSD11B1 deficiency in humans will result in dysregulation of cortisol levels, leading to impaired glucose metabolism and muscle wasting. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring cortisol levels in HSD11B1-deficient patients and comparing them to healthy controls.

We hypothesize that GNAS mutations cause Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 by disrupting the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4) and H3K9. GNAS encodes the GNAS protein, which is a member of the G-protein family. G-proteins are involved in the regulation of gene expression through histone methylation. Specifically, GNAS binds to the histone methyltransferase MLL1 and the histone demethylase LSD1 to form a complex that methylates H3K4 and H3K9. Disruption of this complex by GNAS mutations would lead to decreased methylation of these histones, resulting in aberrant gene expression and the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84.

We hypothesize that NUDT13 deficiency leads to the accumulation of toxic intermediates in the branched-chain amino acid catabolic pathway, resulting in Short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. NUDT13 is a member of the NUDIX superfamily of hydrolases, which catalyze the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate (PPi) from nucleotide substrates. NUDT13 is specifically involved in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids, catalyzing the hydrolysis of PPi from 3-dehydro-2-methyl-butyryl-CoA (DMBCoA) to 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyryl-CoA (HMBCoA). The accumulation of DMBCoA due to NUDT13 deficiency would result in the inhibition of HMBCoA dehydrogenase, leading to the accumulation of HMB and 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyrate (HM2B), which are toxic to the cell.

We hypothesize that CYP2J2 is a key enzyme in the metabolic pathway leading to arterial calcification of infancy, generalized, 1. CYP2J2 is a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily of enzymes, which are involved in the metabolism of steroid hormones, fatty acids, and other lipids. We propose that CYP2J2 is involved in the metabolism of a specific lipid, which is a precursor to a compound that promotes arterial calcification. We predict that inhibition of CYP2J2 activity will result in a decrease in the levels of this lipid precursor, and a subsequent decrease in arterial calcification. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of CYP2J2 activity and the lipid precursor in patients with arterial calcification of infancy, generalized, 1, and comparing them to healthy controls. Inhibition of CYP2J2 activity can be achieved using specific inhibitors, and the effect on arterial calcification can be measured.

We hypothesize that ALOX12B deficiency in humans can lead to mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency 1 (MTPD1) due to the accumulation of arachidonic acid (AA) in mitochondria. AA is an essential fatty acid that is converted to leukotriene B4 (LTB4) by ALOX12B. LTB4 is a potent inflammatory mediator that is produced in response to inflammation and injury. In addition to its role in inflammation, LTB4 is also a potent inhibitor of mitochondrial function. LTB4 has been shown to inhibit mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in a dose-dependent manner. The accumulation of AA in mitochondria in ALOX12B deficiency may lead to the production of LTB4, which in turn may inhibit mitochondrial function, leading to MTPD1.

We hypothesize that KARS1 deficiency leads to impaired mitochondrial translation, resulting in a deficiency of mitochondrial proteins, including the enzyme glutamate formiminotransferase (GFPT2). This would lead to a deficiency of the neurotransmitter glutamate, which is essential for normal brain function. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that KARS1 encodes the mitochondrial enzyme lysyl-tRNA synthetase, which is involved in mitochondrial translation. Additionally, mutations in KARS1 have been associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and neurological symptoms. Furthermore, GFPT2 deficiency has been associated with a deficiency of glutamate, which is essential for normal brain function. This hypothesis can be tested by measuring the levels of glutamate in the brains of patients with KARS1 deficiency and GFPT2 deficiency. If the levels of glutamate are found to be lower in patients with KARS1 deficiency and GFPT2 deficiency compared to controls, this would support the hypothesis that KARS1 deficiency leads to a deficiency of GFPT2, resulting in a deficiency of glutamate.

We hypothesize that ENTPD8 deficiency leads to combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria through a mechanism involving the dephosphorylation of malonate-CoA. Malonate-CoA is a toxic intermediate in the mitochondrial metabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). It is normally detoxified by the enzyme malonate-CoA lyase (MCL), which converts malonate-CoA to pyruvate and CoASH. MCL is allosterically inhibited by acetyl-CoA, and its activity is further inhibited by malonyl-CoA, a product of BCAAs metabolism. We predict that ENTPD8 deficiency leads to the accumulation of malonate-CoA due to the inability to dephosphorylate malonate-CoA-6'-P. The accumulation of malonate-CoA leads to the inhibition of MCL, resulting in the accumulation of malonyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. The accumulation of these two metabolites leads to the inhibition of the mitochondrial BCAA degradation pathway, resulting in the accumulation of BCAAs and their toxic intermediates, including malonate-CoA. The accumulation of malonate-CoA and its toxic intermediate, malonic acid, in the urine is the cause of the combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria phenotype.

We hypothesize that TPO-mediated erythropoiesis is impaired in Erythrocytosis, familial, 8 due to a deficiency in the availability of the substrate, L-tyrosine, for TPO. This deficiency may be due to a mutation in the SLC19A1 gene, which encodes the thiamine transporter THTR-1. THTR-1 is responsible for the uptake of thiamine, which is required for the conversion of L-tyrosine to L-DOPA by THTR-1. L-DOPA is then converted to L-tyrosine by THTR-1. Therefore, a mutation in the SLC19A1 gene may lead to a decrease in the availability of L-tyrosine for TPO, resulting in erythrocytosis.

We hypothesize that ND1 is a key regulator of the inflammatory response in juvenile arthritis. ND1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the electron transport chain. It is also a cofactor for the enzyme arginase, which converts arginine to ornithine and urea. In addition, ND1 has been shown to regulate the activity of the NF-κB pathway, which is a key regulator of the inflammatory response. We predict that in patients with juvenile arthritis, ND1 levels will be elevated in the blood and synovial fluid of the joints affected by the disease. This will lead to increased arginase activity, resulting in decreased levels of arginine, which is an important regulator of the immune response. This will in turn lead to increased inflammation in the joints of patients with juvenile arthritis. To test this hypothesis, we will measure ND1 levels in the blood and synovial fluid of patients with juvenile arthritis and compare them to healthy controls. We will also measure arginine levels in the same samples and compare them between the two groups.

We hypothesize that CYP4F3 is a key enzyme in the metabolic pathway leading to the production of a toxic metabolite that causes axonal demyelination in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, type 2D.
